title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
summary: When the IRS wants information about you from a third party like your employer or bank, current law requires it to notify you in advance — but not what specific information it's seeking. This bill requires the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to collect from the third party, and give you at least 45 days to provide it yourself, whenever the IRS hasn't already asked you for it and you could reasonably provide it. Two exceptions apply: the rule doesn't cover tax collection proceedings, and the Secretary can waive it when third-party contact is deemed necessary.
brief: Requires the IRS to tell taxpayers exactly what information it plans to collect from third parties and give them 45 days to provide it first.

top_lines.headline: Specific Notice Required
subs: IRS must identify each item sought from a third party when the taxpayer hasn't been asked before and could provide it
Taxpayers get at least 45 days to respond — more if they request it with reasonable cause

top_lines.headline: Exceptions
subs: Specificity requirement waived for tax collection proceedings or when Secretary determines third-party contact is necessary regardless

likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor and a narrow taxpayer privacy focus. The IRS exemption allowing the Secretary to waive specificity requirements whenever deemed necessary limits the bill's practical effect, which may reduce the urgency Senate sponsors attach to it. IRS procedural reform bills without broad coalition backing rarely advance quickly in the Senate.

items.main: Names the Act the “Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Specificity of Third-Party Contact Notices

items.main: Amends Section 7602(c)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to require the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to seek from a third party when that information has not been previously requested from the taxpayer and could reasonably be provided by the taxpayer.
items.detail: The advance notice must provide the taxpayer with a period of not less than 45 days — or more if the taxpayer requests additional time and shows reasonable cause — to respond, including by providing the information themselves, before the IRS contacts the third party. The exception in Section 7602(c)(3)(B) provides that the specificity and waiting period requirements do not apply if the information is sought for collection of a tax liability, or if the Secretary determines the third-party information is necessary regardless of whether the taxpayer could provide it. Effective date: 12 months after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill's specificity and 45-day notice requirements do not apply whenever the Secretary determines that the third-party information is necessary, without any standard for what constitutes necessity or any procedural check on that determination.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as expanding taxpayer notification rights. The necessity exception allows the IRS to bypass both the itemized notice and the 45-day waiting period entirely based on the Secretary's own judgment, with no defined standard, independent review, or notification to the taxpayer that the exception has been invoked.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: At its core, this commonsense legislation is a simple due process idea: Before the IRS goes to your bank, your employer, your vendor, or another third party for information about you, when you can reasonably provide that information yourself, you should be told what they are looking for and given a fair chance to respond. Under current law, taxpayers can receive a general third-party contact notice, but too often those notices aren't specific enough to let a person meaningfully respond.

gaps: The bill requires the IRS to give the taxpayer 45 days to respond but does not specify whether the IRS is barred from contacting the third party if the taxpayer provides the requested information within the window.

The bill does not address the taxpayer's right to receive notice that the Secretary has invoked the necessity exception, leaving taxpayers without information about why the standard procedure was not followed.

added: Section 7602(c)(1)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code — requirement for IRS to identify each specific item of information sought from a third party when not previously requested from the taxpayer
Section 7602(c)(1)(C) amendment — 45-day minimum response period before third-party contact, with extensions available on reasonable cause

modified: New specificity duty narrowed — the IRS must itemize info sought from third parties only when it "is related to determining tax liability" (plus the existing not-previously-requested and taxpayer-could-provide tests)

Exception for the Secretary simplified — the specificity rule now does not apply whenever "the Secretary determines that such information is necessary," replacing the two-prong carve-out (collection of a tax liability, or necessity notwithstanding taxpayer availability)
removed: Dropped the phrase letting taxpayers respond "including by providing the information described in subparagraph (B)" from the 45-day response window
Removed the standalone exception for information sought "with respect to the collection of a tax liability"
